claims.text: After 1 hour per day of screen use, higher daily screen time is associated with lower psychological well-being among children and adolescents aged 2 to 17.
Non-users and low users (1 hour per day) of screens generally do not differ in psychological well-being.
Associations between screen time and lower psychological well-being are larger among adolescents than among younger children.
Adolescents aged 14 to 17 with high screen use (7+ hours per day vs 1 hour per day) are more than twice as likely to ever have been diagnosed with depression (RR 2.39).
Adolescents aged 14 to 17 with high screen use (7+ hours per day vs 1 hour per day) are more than twice as likely to ever have been diagnosed with anxiety (RR 2.26).
Adolescents aged 14 to 17 with high screen use (7+ hours per day vs 1 hour per day) are more than twice as likely to have been treated by a mental health professional in the last 12 months (RR 2.22).

Adolescents aged 14 to 17 with high screen use (7+ hours per day vs 1 hour per day) are more than twice as likely to have taken medication for a psychological or behavioral issue in the last 12 months (RR 2.99).
Moderate use of screens (4 hours per day vs 1 hour per day) is associated with lower psychological well-being.

evidence.description: After 1 h/day of use, more hours of daily screen time were associated with lower psychological well-being, including less curiosity, lower self-control, more distractibility, more difficulty making friends, less emotional stability, being more difficult to care for, and inability to finish tasks.
Non-users and low users of screens generally did not differ in well-being.
Associations between screen time and lower psychological well-being were larger among adolescents than younger children.
Among 14- to 17-year-olds, high users of screens (7+ h/day vs. low users of 1 h/day) were more than twice as likely to ever have been diagnosed with depression (RR 2.39, 95% CI 1.54, 3.70).
Among 14- to 17-year-olds, high users of screens (7+ h/day vs. low users of 1 h/day) were more than twice as likely to ever have been diagnosed with anxiety (RR 2.26, CI 1.59, 3.22).

Among 14- to 17-year-olds, high users of screens (7+ h/day vs. low users of 1 h/day) were more than twice as likely to have been treated by a mental health professional (RR 2.22, CI 1.62, 3.03) in the last 12 months.

Among 14- to 17-year-olds, high users of screens (7+ h/day vs. low users of 1 h/day) were more than twice as likely to have taken medication for a psychological or behavioral issue (RR 2.99, CI 1.94, 4.62) in the last 12 months.
Moderate use of screens (4 h/day) was also associated with lower psychological well-being.

methodologies.name: Cross-sectional survey analysis of 2016 NSCH data
methodologies.description: Analyzed caregiver reports from a nationally representative random sample of US children aged 2 to 17, examining associations between daily screen time categories and measures of psychological well-being with demographic controls.
conditions: Excluded children with 8 major conditions (autism, blindness, cerebral palsy, deafness, Down Syndrome, developmental delay, epilepsy, intellectual disability)

limitations.text: Previous research exploring associations between screen time and psychological well-being among children and adolescents has been inconsistent.
Screen time was reported by caregivers and not the children or adolescents themselves, likely resulting in underestimates of screen time.
Due to the cross-sectional design of the study, it is not possible to determine causality between screen time and low psychological well-being.
The survey assessed only weekday screen time and excluded weekend screen time.
The survey items combined TV and electronic games into one question, preventing differentiation between legacy media and digital media.

future_work.text: Public health organizations should consider extending specific screen time limit recommendations to preteens and teens.
Healthcare providers should assess screen time during clinical evaluations to identify children and adolescents at higher risk for mental health issues.
